turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response:
Well, hello Doctor. I suppose I came in because... well, it's about church. I keep doing these odd things there. Like at the potluck table, I'll be standing there holding the serving spoon right up in the air and I just... don't move. Just stuck holding it up. It was the big spoon we use for the mashed potatoes. Martha always makes the potatoes, but she puts way too much butter in them. I told her my stomach can't take all that rich food, but she never listens to a word I say. She's been stubborn since we were girls, always had to have things her way. 

But anyway... people will be waiting in line on me to get their food, and I'll just be standing there folding the exact same stack of napkins over and over again. Just folding and folding. They are those cheap paper napkins, you know? Not the nice cloth ones my mother used to have. She had this beautiful set with little blue daisies on the corners, kept them in a heavy cedar chest. I always loved that cedar smell, it reminds me of the old house we lived in before the county paved the road... but yes, I'm just standing there folding the same napkins while folks are trying to get by.

symptom_reasoning.S021: The patient exhibits tangential speech, wandering off-topic to discuss Martha's potatoes, her mother's cloth napkins, and a cedar chest.
symptom_reasoning.S022: The patient describes abnormal motor behaviors, including freezing in a posture with a serving spoon and repetitively folding the same stack of napkins.

Like I'm just standing there, and my hands are moving. My hands have always been busy, though. Even when I was a little girl, I was always knitting or sewing. I made this beautiful quilt once, all out of scraps from my old dresses. It had all these little squares, pinks and yellows. My sister said it looked like a rag rug, but she was always jealous of my sewing. She couldn't thread a needle to save her life. She married a man who sold insurance, moved out to Omaha... I haven't seen her since our mother passed. But anyway, I don't really know why I fold them like that. I just do.

I made my famous pecan pies for every single one of those sales. I use my grandmother's recipe—the secret is just a little dash of dark molasses in with the corn syrup. Makes it rich. She puts celery in it, which I've always said is a mistake. Celery gets so stringy if you don't chop it fine enough. My mother never used celery, she used sweet pickles. We'd can them ourselves every August. The kitchen would get so hot, just steaming with vinegar and sugar... you'd be sweating clear through your apron by noon. We had this huge heavy kettle for boiling the mason jars, and you had to use these special metal tongs to lift them out so you didn't scald your fingers. My sister Betty burned her wrist awful bad one year doing that. She had to put butter on it, which they say now you aren't supposed to do, but back then everybody put butter on a burn... 

But, oh, what were you asking? About making a decision to sit still? I just... I don't know. I know people are waiting on me while I'm folding and folding, or just holding that spoon up staring at nothing, but I just don't seem to stop myself.

We used to have a polishing party every spring right before Easter Sunday. All the ladies would sit around in the fellowship hall with old soft rags and that pink polish... Wright's Silver Cream, I think it was. It gets all under your fingernails and turns black as soot when you rub the tarnish off. You have to scrub real hard on the handles because they have this little rose pattern stamped into them, and the tarnish just loves to hide in those little grooves. 

My mother had a silver gravy boat with a rose pattern just like it. We only ever brought it out for Thanksgiving and Christmas. I was the one who had to polish it, of course, because my hands were small enough to get around the little spout. If you didn't get every speck of tarnish off that spout, my mother would make you start all over again from the very beginning. She was particular like that. They grow so tall you have to put up chicken wire for them to climb. One year, a groundhog got under the fence and ate near about half my crop before July. My husband sat out there on the back porch with his BB gun for three nights straight trying to scare that thing off. He never did get him, though. The mosquitoes were so bad that summer, he came in covered in welts. We had to rub calamine lotion all over his arms and neck. It dries all pink and chalky, you know, gets all over the bedsheets.
